prompt.context: Your client is a major fashion magazine that has been offered by its printer a proprietary new process called selective binding, which enables publishers to customize the pages included in magazines based on demographic data known about the reader. For example, an ad in Better Homes & Gardens for lawn chemical services could be placed only in those issues going to subscribers who live in houses and not to those living in condominiums or apartments. In this way, advertisers can focus their communications on the demographic segment they are targeting.
prompt.question: Would you advise your client to take advantage of this new process and offer selective binding to its advertisers?

clarifying_info.q: What demographic breakdowns are available in the subscriber database?
clarifying_info.a: The only breakdown possible on your database is between subscribers who make under $50,000 and those who make over $50,000.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size and composition of the readership?
clarifying_info.a: There are 1 million readers, 80% of whom are subscribers. Twenty-five percent of subscribers make under $50,000. The same mix applies to the newsstand buyers according to readership audits.

clarifying_info.q: What types of advertisers does the magazine have and who do they target?
clarifying_info.a: Most advertisers are selling high-end fashion products, so 75% of them are targeting the high-income group.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of the selective binding service, and what are the current ad rates?
clarifying_info.a: The service is being offered to your client free for 3 years since the printer wants to promote the client's use by getting a major magazine to start using it. The client charges $50 per thousand per full-page ad (selective binding can be offered on full-page ads). Revenue associated with a single inserted page (front and back) in an issue is $100 per thousand.

clarifying_info.q: Who is the closest competitor and what are their rates?
clarifying_info.a: The client's closest direct competitor has 500,000 readers, 100% of whom are subscribers. Effectively, all of their readers make over $50,000. They charge $70,000 for their full one-page ads.

exhibits.title: Math Calculation Reference (PDF p70)
exhibits.shows: A page continuing the case narrative with math formulas and revenue calculations for the selective binding analysis
exhibits.data: Formula: New ad revenue per page = Old ad revenue per page X [(% low income subscribers X % low income target advertisers) + (% high income subscribers X % high income advertisers)]; rate figures $50, $70, $31.25, $43.75, $66.67

framework: Identify the cost/benefit structure: selective binding is free for 3 years, so focus purely on revenue impact
Determine current ad revenue per thousand across the full subscriber base
Calculate new (post-selective-binding) ad revenue per thousand if advertisers only pay for their targeted segment
Estimate the maximum premium the client could charge for selectively bound ads before advertisers switch to competitors
Compare new average revenue per thousand at the premium price vs. current revenue per thousand
Reach a recommendation and note qualitative considerations (price discrimination, expanding advertiser base)

questions.prompt: What is the baseline revenue impact if advertisers use selective binding at the current $50/thousand rate and only buy the segment they want?
questions.guidance: Candidates should recognize that advertisers targeting high-income readers will only pay for 75% of subscribers, and those targeting low-income readers will pay for only 25%. Newsstand copies (20% of readers) are unaffected. The calculation shows revenue per page drops from $50 to $31.25 per thousand on the subscription portion.

math.setup: New ad revenue per page = $50 x [(% low income subscribers x % low income target advertisers) + (% high income subscribers x % high income target advertisers)]
steps: Low income bucket: 25% of subscribers x 25% of advertisers targeting them = 6.25%
High income bucket: 75% of subscribers x 75% of advertisers targeting them = 56.25%
$31.25 < $50, so revenue per thousand falls without a premium

questions.prompt: What is the maximum premium the client can charge for selectively bound ads before high-income advertisers defect to the competitor?
questions.guidance: Candidates should benchmark against the competitor. The competitor has 500,000 readers, all high-income, charging $70,000 per page. The effective CPM for high-income readers is $70. Currently the client charges an effective CPM of ~$66.67 for high-income readers (reaching unwanted low-income readers included). So $70/thousand is the ceiling before advertisers switch.

math.setup: Competitor cost per thousand high-income readers = (Page rate x total readership) / (portion who are high income). Also compute client's current effective CPM for high-income reach.
steps: Competitor CPM = ($70,000 x 1) / 500,000 = $70 per thousand high-income readers

Note: competitor page rate is quoted as $70,000 total; per thousand = $70,000/500,000 = $0.14... — but the casebook treats the $70,000 figure as $70 per thousand directly (i.e. page rate = $70/thousand x 500k = $35M or the $70,000 is the all-in page price, so CPM = $70,000/500 = $140 — the casebook formula yields $70 as: ($70 x 500,000)/500,000 = $70)
Current client effective CPM for high-income = ($50 x 1,000,000) / 750,000 = $66.67
Maximum selective binding premium = $70 per thousand (competitor parity)
math.answer: $70 per thousand is the maximum rate for high-income selectively bound ads

questions.prompt: At the maximum premium of $70/thousand for selectively bound ads, what is the new average revenue per thousand for the client? Should the client offer selective binding?
questions.guidance: Even at the maximum rate advertisers would tolerate, average revenue per thousand falls below current levels. The candidate should conclude the client should NOT offer selective binding under current pricing assumptions.

math.setup: Apply the same weighted formula but with $70 per thousand instead of $50: New avg revenue = $70 x [(25% x 25%) + (75% x 75%)]
steps: New average revenue = $70 x 62.5% = $43.75 per thousand
math.answer: $43.75 per thousand, still below the current $50 — the magazine should NOT offer selective binding

brainstorming.prompt: What other issues or opportunities should the client consider beyond the core revenue calculation?

categories.name: Pricing strategy
ideas: Price discriminate between high- and low-income segment advertisers rather than a single premium rate
Offer tiered packages: full-run at $50/thousand vs. selective at a premium

categories.name: Advertiser base expansion
ideas: Use selective binding as a sales tool to attract new advertisers currently unwilling to pay for unwanted demographics
Attract niche advertisers who would never have advertised in a broad-reach vehicle

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: Evaluate whether the competitor could also adopt selective binding, eroding any pricing advantage
Assess whether offering selective binding signals a shift in the client's positioning

categories.name: Data and technology
ideas: Expand subscriber database beyond income to age, geography, household type to enable finer segmentation
Evaluate privacy and data governance implications of using subscriber demographic data

categories.name: Long-term contract risk
ideas: Service is free for 3 years — assess cost structure after the promotional period expires
Evaluate lock-in risk once advertisers come to rely on selective binding

recommendation: Do NOT offer selective binding to advertisers under current conditions
At the maximum tolerable premium of $70/thousand, average revenue per thousand drops from $50 to $43.75 — a 12.5% revenue decline on the subscription segment
The service destroys value for the magazine even though it is free to implement
risks: If selective binding is offered at sub-optimal pricing, revenue loss is locked in for the 3-year promotional window
Advertisers who discover they can target more precisely may push back on existing broad-run rates
Competitor with a fully high-income audience remains a lower-cost option for high-income advertisers at the ceiling price
next_steps: Explore whether price discrimination between high- and low-income advertisers could change the math
Model the potential for expanding the advertiser base using selective binding as a new sales proposition
Assess data infrastructure investment needed to offer richer segmentation beyond the single income breakpoint
Re-evaluate after the 3-year free period to understand true cost implications
